newsitem.title: USA: Jobless claims post surprising drop in latest week.
newsitem.headline: Jobless claims post surprising drop in latest week.

text.p: The number of Americans signing up for first-time unemployment benefits fell sharply last week, the Labour Department said Thursday, reigniting concerns that a tight labour market could trigger inflation.

New filings dropped unexpectedly to 319,000 in the week ended Oct. 5, compared with a revised 341,000 a week earlier. Wall Street economists had predicted that claims in the latest week would inch up to 342,000.

"It represents how fundamentally tight the labour market is," said David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Langston & Co. "And it gives us a hint that labour market conditions are even tighter than we thought."

The inflation-sensitive 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was off more than three-quarters of a point, and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction of its price, climbed to 6.89 percent from 6.83 percent Wednesday.

The latest report stood in contrast to last week's release of September jobs data, which showed the number of jobs shrinking for the first time in eight months. A drop in the number of workers claiming benefits in the latest period suggested that fewer jobs were lost in the first week of October.

The department's four-week moving average of jobless claims -- considered a more accurate gauge of employment trends because it smooths out weekly fluctuations -- fell to 332,250 from the previous week's revised average of 334,750.
"This week's numbers would suggest that the economy is still quite healthy," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc.
Economists have been keeping close tabs on the pace of average hourly earnings growth in recent months as they look for evidence that labour shortages have put upward pressure on wages.

So far, such factors as competition from overseas have worked to limit how much U.S. businesses can boost prices to offset higher labour costs, economists say. But some forecasters expect rising wages to be reflected in the prices consumers pay for goods and services later this year or early next year.
The latest official data on inflation will be released Friday when the Labour Department issues the September producer price index, which tracks inflation at the wholesale level.

In the weekly jobless report, the department said four states and one territory reported decreases in initial claims exceeding 1,000 on an unadjusted basis in the week ended Sept. 28, the latest period for which data were available.
They were North Carolina, with 4,591 fewer filings; Georgia, with 1,550; Florida, with 1,205; and South Carolina, with 1,098. Puerto Rico had 3,574 fewer claims.
North Carolina attributed the falloff in claims to fewer layoffs in the construction and textile industries.
Georgia linked the decrease to fewer layoffs in the textile and food industries, while South Carolina cited fewer layoffs in the food industry.
Florida reported fewer layoffs in the construction, trade and service industries, as well as in manufacturing and agriculture. Puerto Rico had no comment.
Tennessee, with 1,381 additional claims, was the only state reporting an increase in claims exceeding 1,000 in the week.
